subject: Computing
exam: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Computer Science (4CP0)
source: Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2 specification (Topic 3 Computers, Topic 4 Networks); sequence follows the school's Drive Y10-11 scheme of work topics (cyber security, networks) and the Computer Science 9-1 folder; Python practice retained for Paper 2 skills | Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2 specification (syllabus file content/syllabus/ks4/computing.json: units 3.1 to 3.3, 4.1, 4.2, 5.1 to 5.3). Original lessons. The existing y11 set (content/lessons/computing/y11.json) already gives an overview of the CPU and fetch-decode-execute, memory and storage, operating systems and utilities, translators, LAN/WAN, star and mesh topologies, common protocols, malware and network threats, and prevention; these lessons do not re-teach that overview and instead cover the remaining spec points (buses, von Neumann, embedded systems, robust software, internet structure, latency, transmission calculations, TCP/IP layers, bus topology, ethical issues, intellectual property, environmental impact) with deeper, exam-style treatment. | Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel 1CP2 specification

lessons.title: The CPU and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
objectives: Describe the purpose of the CPU and its main components
Explain the fetch-decode-execute cycle
Explain how clock speed, cores and cache affect performance

keywords.def: the central processing unit which carries out program instructions
arithmetic logic unit: does calculations and logical comparisons
directs the flow of data and instructions in the CPU
a very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU
fast memory close to the CPU which holds frequently used data

starter: Bismillah. State two input devices and two output devices.
Why does a program need to be in main memory before it can run?
What does 'processing' mean in input-process-output?

teach.heading: Inside the CPU
bullets: ALU: arithmetic and logic.
Control unit: manages instructions.
Registers: tiny, fast storage.
Cache: fast memory near the CPU.
teach.note: Draw a block diagram with the CPU connected to main memory by buses. Explain that the CPU follows the stored program idea of Von Neumann architecture: instructions and data are stored in the same main memory. Pupils sketch the diagram.

teach.heading: Registers
bullets: PC: address of the next instruction.
MAR: address to read or write.
MDR: data being transferred.
ACC: results of calculations.
teach.note: Walk through what each register holds. A common mistake is to say the PC holds the instruction; it holds the address of the next instruction. Learners should be able to say what each register stores.

teach.heading: Fetch-decode-execute
bullets: Fetch: instruction copied from memory to CPU.
Decode: control unit works out what it means.
Execute: instruction is carried out.
Repeat for the next instruction.
teach.note: Trace a simple instruction 'ADD 5': PC address goes to MAR, the instruction is fetched into MDR, the PC increases, the control unit decodes, the ALU executes and the ACC stores the result. Use the cycle as a loop.

teach.heading: Performance factors
bullets: Clock speed: cycles per second (GHz).
More cores: tasks run in parallel.
Bigger cache: fewer slow memory trips.
teach.note: Explain each factor with consequences. Misconception: more cores always means faster; it only helps when the software can use multiple cores. Embedded systems (in washing machines, cars) have a CPU dedicated to one function; ask for examples.

practice: State the purpose of the ALU. (carries out calculations and logical comparisons)
Which register stores the address of the next instruction to be fetched? (PC)
Why might a computer with a higher clock speed not always be faster?
independent: Draw and label a diagram showing the CPU, main memory and the registers.
Write a numbered description of the fetch-decode-execute cycle in your own words using the names of the registers.
Write a 4-mark answer: 'Explain how the number of cores and the clock speed affect performance.'
exit: What happens in the 'fetch' stage?
Give two ways to increase the performance of a CPU.
lessons.homework: Research the CPU in a modern phone or laptop. State its clock speed, number of cores and cache size and explain what each means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a colour-coded diagram and a card sort for register names. Stretch: explain why cache is faster than RAM but smaller.

lessons.title: Memory and storage
objectives: Distinguish between primary and secondary storage
Compare RAM, ROM, cache and virtual memory
Compare magnetic, solid-state and optical storage

keywords.def: volatile main memory that holds programs and data in use
non-volatile memory holding start-up instructions
loses its contents when power is switched off
non-volatile storage for programs and files for the long term
part of secondary storage used as extra RAM when RAM is full

starter: Bismillah. Describe the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
What is the difference between a bit and a byte?
Why does your computer lose unsaved work if the power cuts out?

teach.heading: Primary memory
bullets: RAM: volatile, read and write, programs in use.
ROM: non-volatile, holds boot instructions.
Cache: very fast, small, near the CPU.
teach.note: Link to the CPU lesson: CPU only works with data in main memory. Use the desk analogy: RAM is your desk (fast access but small and cleared), storage is a filing cabinet. Ask pupils what happens when RAM fills up.

teach.heading: Virtual memory
bullets: RAM full? Move some data to secondary storage.
Swap data back when needed.
Slower than RAM.
teach.note: Explain that virtual memory prevents crashes when RAM is full but slows the computer down because storage is much slower than RAM. Ask pupils to explain why adding more RAM helps.

teach.heading: Secondary storage
bullets: Magnetic: hard disk drives, cheap, large, moving parts.
Solid state: SSD, flash, fast, durable, costly.
Optical: CD, DVD, Blu-ray, portable, slower.
teach.note: Teach by characteristics: capacity, speed, portability, durability, cost, reliability. Hard disks have moving parts, so are more easily damaged by knocks. Solid state storage has no moving parts. Pupils should always relate their choice to the scenario in the question.

teach.heading: Units of data
bullets: 8 bits = 1 byte; 4 bits = 1 nibble.
Kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte.
Each step up is a factor of 1000 (as used in the specification).
teach.note: Practise conversions: 3 GB = 3000 MB; 4500 KB = 4.5 MB. Before the lesson, check the unit convention (1000) in the Edexcel specification and be consistent. Ask pupils to estimate how many 5 MB photos fit on a 64 GB card (12,800).

practice: State two differences between RAM and ROM.
A photographer needs to carry thousands of photos and store them safely. Which secondary storage would you recommend and why?
Convert 2.5 GB to MB. (2500 MB)
independent: Create a comparison table of magnetic, solid state and optical storage using capacity, speed, portability, durability and cost.
Explain in 4 marks why a computer with too little RAM can become slow.
Calculate how many 4 MB files fit on a 2 GB USB stick. (500)
exit: Define 'volatile'.
Give one advantage of solid-state storage over magnetic storage.
lessons.homework: Find the RAM and storage type of a device in your home. Explain whether it is suitable for its purpose.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide an annotated comparison table with icons and a word bank. Stretch: explain why SSDs are often used as the main drive in laptops but hard disks in servers storing large archives.

lessons.title: Software: operating systems and utility software
objectives: Distinguish between system software and application software
Describe the functions of an operating system
Describe the purpose of utility software

keywords.def: software which manages the hardware and runs other programs
programs which carry out tasks for users, such as a word processor
programs which maintain or protect a computer
software that lets the operating system communicate with a hardware device

starter: Bismillah. Name one type of secondary storage and give one advantage.
What is the difference between hardware and software?
Name three programs that you use on a device.

teach.heading: Types of software
bullets: System software: OS and utilities.
Application software: tasks for users.
Applications need an OS to run.
teach.note: Give examples for each type and ask pupils to classify unfamiliar ones: Windows, an antivirus, a spreadsheet, a web browser. Misconception: a web browser is part of the operating system; it is an application.

teach.heading: Operating system functions
bullets: User interface.
Memory management and multitasking.
Managing peripherals and drivers.
File management and security.
teach.note: Link each function to an example: a window system for the interface; sharing RAM among apps; a printer driver; folders; user accounts and passwords. A strong exam answer states the function and explains what the OS does.

teach.heading: Utility software
bullets: Antivirus: finds and removes malware.
Firewall: filters network traffic.
Backup: copies data for safety.
Compression: makes files smaller.
teach.note: Add disk defragmentation for hard disks (reorders fragmented files) and encryption software. Explain why backups matter: protect against hardware failure, accidental deletion and ransomware. Link to amanah: we look after people's data.

teach.heading: Exam-style link
bullets: Scenario: a school with 1000 pupils.
Which OS functions are needed?
Which utilities are essential?
teach.note: Practise applying knowledge to a context. For example, multi-user accounts and file permissions are important so pupils cannot see teachers' files. Ask them to justify the importance of regular updates.

practice: Classify: Windows, a spreadsheet, a firewall, a game. (OS, application, utility, application)
Describe two functions of an operating system.
Why is a backup important?
independent: Create a table listing five OS functions with a one-line explanation and an example for each.
Explain the difference between application software and system software with two examples of each.
Write a 4-mark answer about why a business should use antivirus software and regular backups.
exit: What is a device driver?
Give two examples of utility software and say what they do.
lessons.homework: List the utility software on a home computer or phone and explain what each does. If you cannot find any, research what built-in tools do the same job.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sorting activity with icons for system and application software. Stretch: explain how multitasking appears to run several programs at the same time.

lessons.title: Programming languages and translators
objectives: Compare high-level and low-level languages
Describe the purpose of a compiler, interpreter and assembler
Choose a suitable language or translator for a situation

keywords.def: a language close to human language, such as Python
a language close to the machine: machine code or assembly
translates the whole program into machine code before it runs
translates and runs a program one line at a time
translates assembly language into machine code

starter: Bismillah. Name two functions of an operating system.
What language have you used for programming in Python lessons?
Why can't a CPU run Python code directly?

teach.heading: High-level languages
bullets: Examples: Python, Java, C#.
Easier to read, write and debug.
Not tied to one type of CPU.
Must be translated before the CPU runs it.
teach.note: Show the same task in Python and in assembly pseudocode to illustrate the difference. Emphasise portability of high-level code. Misconception: Python is not 'run directly by the computer'.

teach.heading: Low-level languages
bullets: Machine code: binary instructions for the CPU.
Assembly: short mnemonics like ADD, LDA.
Hard to write; specific to the CPU.
Used where speed and hardware control matter.
teach.note: Give uses: embedded systems, device drivers, parts of operating systems. The CPU only understands machine code in binary. Assembly needs an assembler.

teach.heading: Compiler vs interpreter
bullets: Compiler: translates all code first, creates a file to run.
Interpreter: translates one line at a time.
Compiled programs run faster.
Interpreters help find errors line by line.
teach.note: Use the analogy of translating a whole book beforehand (compiler) versus a live interpreter in a meeting. Python is usually interpreted when run in a shell. The source code is not needed once a program is compiled, which helps protect it.

teach.heading: Choosing
bullets: Learning to program: high-level + interpreter.
Games with high speed: compiled language.
Tiny embedded device: low-level language.
teach.note: Practise exam-style scenario questions: they require a choice and a reason. Remind pupils that 'it is faster' alone is a weak answer; they should link to the context.

practice: State one advantage and one disadvantage of low-level languages.
Which translator converts assembly language to machine code? (assembler)
Explain why an interpreter is useful when testing a program.
independent: Create a table comparing compiler and interpreter with at least four points.
Explain why a game developer might use a compiled language but a student might use an interpreted language.
Write a 6-mark answer comparing high-level and low-level languages.
exit: What is the only language the CPU can run directly?
State one difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
lessons.homework: Research one embedded system (such as a washing machine). Explain why its programmers might use a low-level language.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a flow diagram showing source code to translator to machine code and a word bank. Stretch: explain what happens when a compiled program contains a syntax error.

lessons.title: Network types, topologies and performance
objectives: Distinguish between LANs and WANs
Describe star and mesh topologies, with advantages and disadvantages
Explain factors that affect network performance

keywords.def: local area network covering a small area such as a school
wide area network covering a large geographical area
the layout of devices and connections in a network
the amount of data that can be sent in a given time

starter: Bismillah. Name one compiler or interpreter and say what it does.
What is the difference between the internet and the web?
How many devices are connected to your home network?

teach.heading: LANs and WANs
bullets: LAN: small area, owned by one organisation.
WAN: large area, often uses third-party links.
The internet is the largest WAN.
teach.note: Give examples: a school network (LAN), a bank linking branches across the UK (WAN). Ask pupils which type they use at home. A common error is to say WAN is 'wireless'; it is about size, not wireless.

teach.heading: Star topology
bullets: Every device connects to a central switch.
A cable failure affects only one device.
Easy to add devices.
If the switch fails, the whole network fails.
teach.note: Draw the star and tick the advantages. Collisions are reduced because the switch sends data only to the intended device. Cost: more cable and a switch.

teach.heading: Mesh topology
bullets: Devices connect to many others.
Data has alternative routes.
Very reliable.
Expensive and complex.
teach.note: Explain full mesh versus partial mesh and why the internet is mesh-like, giving resilience. Compare the number of connections needed as devices increase. Exam answers compare in context.

teach.heading: Performance factors
bullets: Bandwidth.
Number of users.
Transmission media: copper, fibre, wireless.
Interference and distance.
teach.note: Link each factor to an effect on speed: many users share bandwidth; fibre is faster than copper; Wi-Fi suffers from interference and walls. Compare wired and wireless: wired is more stable and secure, wireless is more convenient and mobile.

practice: Is a network linking two mosque centres in different cities a LAN or a WAN? (WAN)
State one advantage and one disadvantage of a star network.
Give two reasons why a wired connection may be better than Wi-Fi for a gaming PC.
independent: Draw a star and a mesh network with 5 devices and label the switch/connections.
Compare star and mesh in a table with advantages, disadvantages and one use for each.
Write a 6-mark answer recommending a network type and topology for a school with 200 computers.
exit: Define 'bandwidth'.
State one advantage of a mesh topology.
lessons.homework: Draw the network in your home (router, devices, connection to the internet) and say whether it is a LAN. Explain which devices are wired or wireless.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide topology diagrams to label and a table with icons for advantages and disadvantages. Stretch: calculate the number of cables needed for a full mesh of 6 devices (15).

lessons.title: Network protocols and hardware
objectives: Describe the purpose of common protocols
Explain how data is sent as packets across a network
Describe the role of network hardware

keywords.def: a set of rules for how devices communicate
a number identifying a device on a network
domain name system: converts website names into IP addresses
a device that forwards packets between networks
a device that connects devices in a LAN and sends data to the correct one

starter: Bismillah. Name two topologies and state one advantage of each.
Why are rules needed when different devices communicate?
What happens when you type a web address into a browser? Describe the first step.

teach.heading: Why protocols?
bullets: Devices from different makers must understand each other.
Protocols set the rules.
Each protocol has a job.
teach.note: Use the analogy of languages and postal rules. Without agreed rules, communication fails. Link to the Y4 packet activity: packets have addresses and are reassembled.

teach.heading: Common protocols
bullets: HTTP/HTTPS: web pages (HTTPS is encrypted).
FTP: transferring files.
SMTP: sending email.
IMAP/POP: receiving email.
TCP/IP: sending packets across the internet.
teach.note: Learners should match each protocol with its purpose. Misconception: HTTPS means a site is trustworthy; it only means the connection is encrypted. Check the specification for the exact list required.

teach.heading: Packets and addresses
bullets: Data is split into packets.
Each packet has source and destination IP addresses.
Packets can take different routes.
TCP reassembles them in order.
teach.note: Explain that IP addresses are logical and can change, whereas MAC addresses are fixed to a device's network card. DNS works like a phone book converting names to IP addresses. Walk through the sequence from typing a URL to receiving a page.

teach.heading: Network hardware
bullets: NIC: connects a device to a network.
Switch: connects devices in a LAN.
Router: connects networks.
WAP: wireless access point.
teach.note: Draw a home network: a router with built-in switch and WAP. Ask what each does. A router uses IP addresses to forward packets; a switch uses MAC addresses on a LAN.

practice: Which protocol is used to send email? (SMTP)
Why do packets carry a destination IP address?
State the difference between a switch and a router.
independent: Create a table of five protocols with their purposes and an example of use.
Explain in 4 marks how a web page is requested using DNS and HTTPS and delivered as packets.
Draw a network diagram showing a router, a switch, three computers, a printer and a wireless access point.
exit: What does DNS do?
State the purpose of HTTPS.
lessons.homework: Use the command prompt or an online tool to look up an IP address for a website (for example with nslookup). Record the website name and the address, and describe how DNS helped.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a matching activity for protocols and a labelled diagram of a network. Stretch: explain the difference between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and why IPv6 was developed.

lessons.title: Network security: threats
objectives: Describe common network threats and how they work
Explain how social engineering tricks people
Describe the impact of attacks on organisations

keywords.def: malicious software designed to damage or gain access to a system
fake emails or messages used to trick people into giving information
manipulating people into giving away information or access
flooding a server with requests so legitimate users cannot access it
trying many passwords until the correct one is found

starter: Bismillah. State the purpose of a router.
Name two ways that data on a network could be put at risk.
Why might someone want to steal data from a company?

teach.heading: Malware
bullets: Virus: attaches to files and spreads when they are run.
Worm: spreads itself across networks.
Trojan: pretends to be useful software.
Ransomware: locks files and demands payment.
Spyware: records activity.
teach.note: Distinguish carefully: viruses need a host file and user action; worms replicate on their own. Misconception: a Trojan is a virus; it is distinguished by disguise. Mention that paying a ransom is never guaranteed to restore files.

teach.heading: Attacks on networks
bullets: Brute force: guessing passwords.
Denial of service: overwhelming a server.
Data interception: stealing data in transit.
SQL injection: harmful code typed into a form.
teach.note: Explain each simply. SQL injection happens when a web form allows database commands to be entered. A DoS uses one source; DDoS uses many. Show how long, complex passwords make brute force harder.

teach.heading: Social engineering
bullets: Phishing emails and texts.
Pretending to be IT support.
Shoulder surfing: watching someone type a password.
People are the weakest link.
teach.note: Show a phishing example with clues: urgent tone, strange sender, link that does not match, requests for private data. Link to honesty and amanah: attackers exploit trust, and we protect trust by being careful.

teach.heading: Impact
bullets: Lost or stolen data.
Financial loss and fines.
Damaged reputation.
Downtime.
teach.note: Use a scenario of a hospital or school being hit by ransomware. Ask pupils to name stakeholders affected. Exam answers describe the cause and the effect in context.

practice: Which type of malware spreads itself without the user opening a file? (worm)
Explain how a denial of service attack stops a website working.
Give two clues that an email is phishing.
independent: Create a table of six threats with a one-line description and the possible effect on a business.
Write a 4-mark answer explaining how social engineering might be used to gain access to a company network.
Read a scenario about a school hit by ransomware and list three consequences.
exit: Define phishing.
State one difference between a virus and a worm.
lessons.homework: Find a real news report about a cyber attack. Summarise what happened, the type of attack and the impact in 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide threat cards with pictures to match with descriptions. Stretch: explain why DDoS attacks are harder to block than DoS attacks.

lessons.title: Network security: prevention and the law
objectives: Describe methods of protecting networks and data
Explain how encryption, firewalls and authentication work
State the purpose of the Computer Misuse Act 1990

keywords.def: filters incoming and outgoing network traffic using rules
scrambling data so only authorised people can read it
proving who you are, such as with a password or fingerprint
authorised attempts to break into a system to find weaknesses

starter: Bismillah. Name three types of malware and give one feature of each.
What is social engineering?
How can a user make a password harder to guess?

teach.heading: Protecting systems
bullets: Anti-malware software.
Firewalls.
Software updates and patches.
Backups.
teach.note: Link each prevention to the threat it stops. Anti-malware finds known malware; updates fix vulnerabilities; firewalls block unwanted traffic; backups allow recovery. Prevention is layered: no single method is enough.

teach.heading: Authentication and access
bullets: Strong passwords and two-factor authentication.
Biometrics: fingerprints, face.
Access levels: different rights for different users.
Physical security: locks, ID cards.
teach.note: Explain access levels: pupils can read some folders, teachers can write, administrators control everything. Biometrics are hard to copy but can raise privacy concerns. Add CAPTCHA only if the spec lists it.

teach.heading: Encryption
bullets: Plain text is scrambled to cipher text.
A key is used to scramble and unscramble.
Protects data in transit and storage.
HTTPS uses encryption.
teach.note: Demonstrate a Caesar shift of 3: 'ILM' becomes 'LOP'. Show decryption with the key. Explain that modern encryption is far stronger but follows the same idea: algorithm plus key. Misconception: encryption stops hackers from intercepting data; it stops them reading it.

teach.heading: Testing and the law
bullets: Penetration testing finds weaknesses.
Computer Misuse Act 1990: unauthorised access is illegal.
Data Protection Act 2018: protect personal data.
teach.note: Explain ethical hackers have permission, which makes their testing legal. The Computer Misuse Act covers unauthorised access, access with intent to commit further offences and unauthorised modification of data. Link to the Islamic value of keeping trusts (amanah) when handling others' data.

practice: Encrypt the word CAT using a Caesar shift of 1. (DBU)
State two ways to prevent unauthorised access to a school network.
Why is penetration testing legal when hacking is not?
independent: Create a table matching five threats with the best prevention methods and a reason for each.
Write a 6-mark answer: 'A company stores customer data on a network. Discuss how it can protect the data.'
Write pseudo-code for a program that asks for a password, allows 3 attempts, and prints 'Locked' after 3 failures.
exit: What is the purpose of a firewall?
Give one offence covered by the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
lessons.homework: Review your own online security. List three improvements you or your family could make and which threat each would reduce.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a matching grid of threats and defences with icons. Stretch: write a Python function that encrypts a message with a Caesar shift of a given key.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.1: Computers: architecture, memory and storage
lessons.title: Von Neumann architecture and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a computer carry out a program one tiny step at a time?
objectives: Describe the von Neumann stored-program concept, RAM, CPU components, clock and buses (3.1.1)
Trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle through the registers
Explain how clock speed, cores and cache affect performance
successCriteria: All: name the main CPU components and state their jobs
Most: describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle using register names
Some: trace a short program and explain how architecture affects performance
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: electrical signals and timing
lessons.smsc: Cultural: admiration for the ingenuity of people who made a general machine from simple parts

keywords.def: instructions and data are held in the same memory and fetched by the CPU
a very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU
a set of wires that carries data, addresses or control signals
a signal that sets the speed at which the CPU works, measured in hertz
the cycle in which the CPU gets, understands and carries out an instruction

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between RAM and ROM?
State what the control unit does.
Write 3 GHz in cycles per second.

teach.heading: Stored-program concept
bullets: Program and data are in the same memory (RAM)
The CPU fetches instructions one at a time
Changing the program means changing memory, not rewiring
teach.note: Explain that before this idea computers were rewired for each task. RAM is volatile: it holds the programs and data in use and is lost when power is off. Ask pupils why a general-purpose computer is possible with this idea. The existing y11 lesson 1 introduces the CPU parts; here we link them through buses and the cycle.

head: Part
Job
rows: Tiny fast storage for addresses, data, instruction and results
Fast memory holding frequently used instructions and data
Sets the pace: one cycle per tick

teach.heading: Buses
bullets: Address bus: carries the memory address (one way)
Data bus: carries data and instructions (two ways)
Control bus: carries commands such as read or write
teach.note: Link each bus to the registers: the MAR places an address on the address bus; the MDR receives or sends data on the data bus. Use an analogy of a postal system with addresses, parcels and instructions. Pupils often say the address bus is two-way; it is one-way, from the CPU to memory.

left.title: Address bus
points: Says where to read or write
Width limits the memory that can be addressed

right.title: Data bus
points: Carries the data or instruction itself
Width sets how many bits move at once

teach.heading: Fetch-decode-execute in code
bullets: PC holds the address of the next instruction
Fetch it into CIR and add 1 to PC
Decode it, then execute it
teach.note: Trace the simulation with the class: the program is stored as text so you can see the fetch step. At each pass, PC goes up by one before the instruction is carried out. Ask pupils which line is the fetch (cir = program[pc]) and which the decode (split) and which the execute (the if chain). It is a simplified model that ignores MAR and MDR.

code.text:
program = ["LOAD 5", "ADD 3", "ADD 4"]
acc = 0
pc = 0
while pc < len(program):
    cir = program[pc]
    pc = pc + 1
    op, value = cir.split()
    if op == "LOAD":
        acc = int(value)
    elif op == "ADD":
        acc = acc + int(value)
    print("PC", pc, "CIR", cir, "ACC", acc)
code.output:
PC 1 CIR LOAD 5 ACC 5
PC 2 CIR ADD 3 ACC 8
PC 3 CIR ADD 4 ACC 12

teach.heading: Worked example: one cycle in registers
teach.note: Model with registers on the board as boxes. Say each transfer aloud. Pupils should use the register names in exam answers. Add that the cycle then repeats for the next instruction, millions of times per second.

model.problem: The PC holds 2 and memory address 2 holds the instruction ADD 3. Describe the fetch stage in terms of registers.
steps: The address in the PC (2) is copied to the MAR
The control unit sends a read signal on the control bus
The instruction at address 2 travels on the data bus to the MDR, then is copied to the CIR
The PC is increased by 1, so it holds 3 and points to the next instruction
model.answer: After the fetch, the CIR holds ADD 3 and the PC holds 3. The instruction is then decoded and executed.

teach.heading: Check: performance factors
teach.note: Answer D. Cache holds recently used data close to the CPU, so fewer slow trips to RAM. A would need a bigger hard drive, which is not the CPU. B (a bigger monitor) does not affect speed and C describes a different factor.

check.q: Which change would most directly reduce the number of slow trips the CPU makes to RAM?
check.why: A larger cache stores more frequently used instructions and data next to the CPU. Hard drive size (A), screen size (B) and the cable (C) do not affect how often the CPU goes to RAM.

practice: State one difference between the address bus and the data bus.
A CPU has a clock speed of 2 GHz. State how many cycles it completes each second.
Name the register that stores the address of the next instruction and the register that holds the instruction being decoded.
independent: Core: Write the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle and, for each, say what happens in the CPU.
Extend: Trace the simulation program for program = ['LOAD 2', 'ADD 9', 'ADD 10'] and state the final ACC.
Stretch: Explain why a dual-core CPU with a lower clock speed can still be faster than a single-core CPU with a higher clock speed, and when it would not be.
exit: What does the stored-program concept mean?
Name two registers and state the job of each.
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled diagram of the CPU, RAM and the three buses, and use arrows to show what travels on each when an instruction is fetched.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a diagram with boxes for CPU parts and a word bank. Stretch: ask for an explanation of how the width of the address bus limits RAM.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.1: Computers: architecture, memory and storage
lessons.title: Secondary storage and embedded systems
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does data live when the power goes off, and where are computers hidden in plain sight?
objectives: Explain how magnetic, optical and solid-state secondary storage store data (3.1.2)
Compare the three types for a given scenario
Describe embedded systems and their uses (3.1.3)
successCriteria: All: name the three types of secondary storage and give an example of each
Most: explain how each stores data and compare them
Some: recommend a storage type and justify it with capacity, speed, durability, cost and portability
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: magnetism, light and electrical charge
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship: choosing durable devices and not discarding them lightly

keywords.def: non-volatile storage that keeps data when the power is off
stores data as magnetised areas on a spinning disk
stores data as pits and lands read by a laser
stores data in flash memory with no moving parts
a computer built into a larger device to do a dedicated job

starter: Bismillah. State why RAM is not used to keep your homework saved.
What does non-volatile mean?
Name two examples of devices with a computer inside that are not laptops.

teach.heading: How each type stores data
bullets: Magnetic: platters, magnetised areas, read/write head
Optical: laser reflects differently from pits and lands
Solid state: flash cells trap an electrical charge
teach.note: Describe each mechanism in one sentence and have pupils say the key word: magnetised, reflected, charge. Hard disks spin and the head moves across the platter, so they have moving parts. In an optical disc, a pit scatters the laser light and a land reflects it, giving 0 and 1. SSDs have no moving parts, so are faster and silent.

head: Type
How data is stored
Example
rows: Magnetised areas on a spinning platter
Pits and lands read by a laser

teach.heading: Comparing the types
bullets: Magnetic: large and cheap per GB, slower, fragile
Optical: portable and cheap discs, low capacity
Solid state: fast, durable, quiet, costs more per GB
teach.note: Draw a comparison table with rows capacity, speed, durability, cost, portability. In exam answers pupils must link the feature to the scenario. Avoid vague words such as 'better'; use specific comparisons (for example 'faster to read and write').

teach.heading: Embedded systems
bullets: A computer inside a larger device
Does one dedicated job, often in real time
Examples: washing machine, car engine, pacemaker, smart meter
teach.note: Contrast with a laptop: general purpose, many programs, user installs software. An embedded system has a single fixed purpose, a small processor, little memory, low power and is often reliable and cheap. The program is stored in ROM or flash. Ask pupils to find five embedded systems at home.

right.title: Embedded system
points: Program fixed in ROM or flash

teach.heading: Worked example: recommend storage
teach.note: Model: identify the key requirement in the scenario (cost per GB, durability, size), then match it and give a reason. A good answer states one limitation of the choice. Check understanding by asking what would change if the data were needed hourly.

model.problem: A madrasah wants to store 8 TiB of recorded lessons as a cheap archive that is rarely used. Recommend a type of secondary storage and justify it.
steps: Requirement: very large capacity at a low cost per GB
Magnetic hard disks give large capacity cheaply
Speed is not important because the archive is rarely used
Limitation: moving parts are fragile, so keep a backup
model.answer: Magnetic hard disk drives, because they give the most capacity per pound for rarely accessed data.

teach.heading: Check: embedded or not?
teach.note: Answer B. A microwave oven has a processor built in for one dedicated job: an embedded system. A laptop, a games console and a desktop PC are general-purpose or multi-purpose. Some pupils think a games console is embedded; it runs many programs.

check.q: Which of these is an embedded system?
options: The controller inside a microwave oven
A desktop PC in a computer room
A tablet used to browse the web
check.why: The microwave controller is built into the device and does one dedicated job. The laptop, desktop and tablet run many different programs chosen by the user.

practice: Explain how an optical disc stores a binary 1 and a 0.
Give two reasons why an SSD is better than a hard disk drive in a school laptop.
State two features that make a controller in a heart pacemaker an embedded system.
independent: Core: Complete a table comparing magnetic, optical and solid-state storage for capacity, speed, durability and cost.
Extend: A photographer needs a portable store that survives being dropped in a bag. Recommend a type and justify it in three sentences.
Stretch: A car has about 80 embedded systems. Explain why using embedded systems rather than one general-purpose computer is a sensible design, giving two benefits and one drawback.
exit: Name the type of storage that uses a laser.
Give one example of an embedded system and its dedicated job.
lessons.homework: List ten things in your home that contain an embedded system. For three of them, say what the system does and why it needs no keyboard.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give labelled pictures of each storage type for matching to the key word. Stretch: ask for an evaluation of cloud storage against local storage. This lesson builds on y11 lesson 2 (memory and storage) by adding the mechanisms and embedded systems.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.2: Computers: operating systems, utilities and robust software
lessons.title: Operating systems and utility software
lessons.bigQuestion: What does the software you never see do to keep a computer working?
objectives: Describe the functions of an operating system: file, process, peripheral and user management (3.2.1)
Describe utility software: repair, backup, compression, defragmentation and anti-malware (3.2.2)
Match functions and utilities to a scenario
successCriteria: All: name four functions of an operating system
Most: describe the job of each utility
Some: recommend which OS functions and utilities a given organisation needs and why
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: managing users and data in an organisation
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah in managing other people's accounts and files fairly and securely

keywords.def: system software that manages the hardware and runs other programs
a program in execution
software that lets the operating system control a peripheral
programs that maintain, protect or tidy a computer system
rearranging file pieces on a hard disk so they are stored together

starter: Bismillah. State the difference between system software and application software.
Name two utility programs you have used.
Why can many programs seem to run at the same time on one CPU?

teach.heading: Four jobs of the operating system
bullets: File management: names, folders, access
Process management: share the CPU and memory
Peripheral management: drivers and buffers
User management: accounts and permissions
teach.note: The existing y11 lesson 3 gives an overview; this lesson gives the detail needed for the longer answers. Process management: the OS decides which program runs in each tiny slice of time (multitasking) and gives each its own memory so they do not overwrite each other. Peripheral management: a driver translates between OS and device. User management: log in, permissions, quotas.

head: Function
Detail
Example
rows: Create, name, move, delete, organise in folders; set permissions
Saving a document into a folder
A file downloads while you browse
Control devices using drivers; buffer data
Sending a document to a printer
A pupil cannot open teachers' files

teach.heading: Utility software
bullets: Repair: fixes errors in files or the system
Backup: copies data for recovery
Compression: makes files smaller
Defragmentation and anti-malware
teach.note: Defragmentation applies to hard disk drives: files get split into fragments scattered over the disk and the utility rearranges them. It is not needed on SSDs, which have no moving head to travel. Show the before and after table on the next slide. Anti-malware scans for and removes harmful software.

left.title: Maintain the system
points: Repair: fix corrupt files and settings

right.title: Protect the data
points: Anti-malware: detect and remove malicious software

teach.heading: Defragmentation
bullets: Before: pieces of each file scattered
After: each file stored together
Fewer head movements, so faster reading
teach.note: Read the blocks out loud: A is a file stored in three pieces. After the utility runs, A is stored in blocks 1 to 3. The read head on a hard disk no longer has to jump around. Ask why it would be pointless on an SSD.

teach.heading: Worked example: match to a scenario
teach.note: Model by underlining the need in the scenario and naming the function or utility, then the reason. Remind pupils that anti-malware does not replace a backup. Ask which function of the OS lets two staff share one computer without seeing each other's files.

model.problem: A madrasah office computer has a slow hard disk, is shared by three staff and holds the only copy of the fee records. Name suitable OS functions and utilities.
steps: Slow hard disk with scattered files: defragmentation
Three staff sharing: user management (separate accounts and permissions)
Only copy of the fee records: backup utility
Protection from harmful files: anti-malware
model.answer: User management, defragmentation, backup and anti-malware, each linked to its need.

teach.heading: Check: which function?
teach.note: Answer C. A driver is software that lets the OS communicate with a device, so this is peripheral management. A concerns folders and files; B concerns time slices; D concerns accounts.

check.q: A new printer will not work until a driver is installed. Which operating system function is this part of?
check.why: Drivers and device communication belong to peripheral management. File management (A) concerns files and folders; process management (B) concerns running programs; user management (D) concerns accounts and permissions.

practice: Give two examples of what the operating system does in process management.
Explain what defragmentation does and why it helps a hard disk drive.
State one reason why compression utility software is useful when emailing files.
independent: Core: Complete a table with five utilities and one sentence on the purpose of each.
Extend: A school has 600 pupils sharing 40 computers. Describe four operating system functions it relies on, with an example for each.
Stretch: A pupil says 'I do not need a backup because I have anti-malware.' Explain why they are wrong, with two different ways in which data could be lost.
exit: Name the four functions of an operating system covered today.
State which type of drive benefits from defragmentation.
lessons.homework: Write 150 words on what would happen to a school if its operating system had no user management.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sorting task: cards with functions and cards with examples. Stretch: ask for a comparison of full and incremental backup.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.2: Computers: operating systems, utilities and robust software
lessons.title: Robust software, audit trails and code reviews
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we build software that does not break, and find its weak points before an attacker does?
objectives: Explain what makes software robust (3.2.3)
Describe how audit trails help to find vulnerabilities
Describe how code reviews find faults and weaknesses
successCriteria: All: define robust software and give two features of it
Most: explain how audit trails and code reviews each find problems
Some: analyse a log or a piece of code and identify the weakness
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: quality assurance and risk management
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah and honesty: building software people can safely trust, and reporting faults you find

keywords.def: software that keeps working correctly even with unexpected input or errors
a weakness that could be exploited to cause harm
a record of who did what and when on a system
examining source code, usually by another person, to find faults and weaknesses

starter: Bismillah. What does validation check?
Give one example of boundary test data.
State what a log file is.

teach.heading: Robust software
bullets: Handles unexpected input without crashing
Validates data and checks for errors
Is well structured, tested and maintained
teach.note: Robust is not the same as bug-free; it means that faults and strange input do not cause failure or a security hole. Show the function: bad input gets a safe response. Ask what would happen if the function used int(text) directly. A crash or a vulnerability.

teach.heading: Features of robust design
bullets: Validate every input
Break the program into tested subprograms
Handle errors with safe messages
Update and patch known flaws
teach.note: Tie each feature to a threat: validation stops bad input; subprograms are easier to test; error handling avoids leaking system details; patching closes known holes. Common exam error: 'robust means it never crashes'. Stress 'continues to work correctly or fails safely'.

left.title: Fragile software
points: Assumes the user types sensible input

teach.heading: Audit trails
bullets: A log of actions: who, what, when
Used to find suspicious behaviour
Also used to trace how a fault happened
teach.note: Read the log as a class. Ask what looks suspicious (five failed logins from one account at 02:14 then a success). An audit trail does not stop an attack; it helps to detect it and investigate afterwards. Link to accountability and to Data Protection duties.

teach.heading: Worked example: audit trail and code review
teach.note: Model the two methods side by side. Emphasise that a code review is done before release, by someone other than the author, who looks for faults and for vulnerabilities such as missing validation. The audit trail is evidence after the event. Point out that both are needed.

model.problem: Use the log above to explain what an audit trail shows, and describe what a code review of the login code might find.
steps: Log: three failed logins in 25 seconds, then success, then a download of fee records
Suggests guessing a password; it shows when and which account
Code review: a second programmer reads the login code
Might find no limit on attempts and no lock-out, so the weakness can be fixed before release
model.answer: The audit trail shows evidence of a possible attack; the code review finds the weakness that allowed it.

teach.heading: Check: audit trail or code review?
teach.note: Answer A. An audit trail records events as they happen, so it can be examined afterwards. B describes a code review. C is testing, D is validation. Make the point that pupils must name the right method for the right job.

check.q: Which statement correctly describes an audit trail?
options: A record of user actions that can be examined to find suspicious activity
A programmer reading source code to find weaknesses before release
A set of test data used to check a program
A check that a value lies within a range
check.why: An audit trail logs who did what and when. Reading code before release is a code review (B); test data (C) and range checks (D) are different ideas.

practice: State two features of robust software.
Explain how a code review helps to make software more secure.
A log shows 200 failed login attempts from one account in a minute. State what this suggests and what the school should do.
independent: Core: Write a short definition of each: robust software, audit trail, code review.
Extend: Write a Python function that returns True only if a string is exactly 6 digits, and list the test data you would use to prove it is robust.
Stretch: A bank's mobile app crashes when a user enters a negative amount. Discuss, in 100 words, how robust design, a code review and an audit trail would each help.
exit: Define robust software.
State one thing an audit trail records.
lessons.homework: Look up an example of a software failure in the news (a bug or a data breach). Write 100 words on which robust-software practice might have prevented it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the log table with the suspicious rows highlighted and a sentence frame. Stretch: ask for a comparison of a code review with automated testing.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.3: Computers: programming languages and translators
lessons.title: Programming languages and translators: comparing and choosing
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do we write in one language but the computer runs another?
objectives: Compare the characteristics and purposes of low-level and high-level languages (3.3.1)
Explain how interpreters and compilers translate high-level code differently (3.3.2)
Choose a language and translator for a scenario, with reasons
successCriteria: All: state one difference between high-level and low-level languages
Most: compare a compiler and an interpreter on four points
Some: justify a choice of language and translator for a scenario
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: the idea of a precise symbolic language
lessons.smsc: Moral: accuracy and precision in expressing instructions

keywords.def: binary instructions that the CPU can run directly
a low-level language using mnemonics, one for each machine instruction
translates assembly language into machine code
translates the whole program into machine code before it runs
translates and runs a program one statement at a time

starter: Bismillah. Name one high-level language.
What is machine code made of?
State what a translator does.

teach.heading: Levels of language
bullets: High-level: close to English, easy to learn
Assembly: short codes, one per machine instruction
Machine code: binary the CPU runs directly
teach.note: The existing y11 lesson 4 introduces these; today we compare them precisely. Show one high-level statement against its low-level steps. Note that one high-level line becomes many machine instructions. Assembly and machine code are specific to a type of processor; high-level code is portable once translated.

head: Level
Example
Translated by
rows: LDA a / ADD b / STA total
Not translated: the CPU runs it

teach.heading: Compare the language types
bullets: High-level: portable, easier to write and debug
Low-level: fast, small, direct control of hardware
Low-level suits device drivers and embedded systems
teach.note: Exam answers need purposes as well as characteristics: for example drivers or tiny embedded controllers use low-level because of memory limits and direct hardware access. Ask pupils which they would use for a web app (high-level).

right.title: Low-level
points: Efficient use of memory and speed

teach.heading: Compiler and interpreter
bullets: Compiler: translates everything first, then runs
Interpreter: translates and runs line by line
Interpreter stops at the first error it reaches
teach.note: The program prints two lines, then crashes at the third. An interpreter shows the earlier output because it had already run those lines. A compiler would report errors before producing anything to run, and the compiled file runs without the compiler. The Python used in this course is usually interpreted, although in practice it first compiles to a simplified form: say this is a simplification for the exam.

code.text:
print("Line 1 runs")
print("Line 2 runs")
print(1 / 0)
print("Line 4 never runs")
code.output:
Line 1 runs
Line 2 runs
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

teach.heading: Worked example: choose a translator
teach.note: Model the structure: need, then choice, then reason. Add the drawback so the answer is balanced. A compiler gives a standalone file so the source code is not given away; an interpreter is quicker for testing.

model.problem: A company will sell a game to thousands of customers and does not want to share its source code. Which translator should it use, and why?
steps: The game is released to customers who do not have the source code
A compiler produces a standalone executable file
The compiled file runs quickly and keeps the source code private
Drawback: it must be recompiled for each type of computer
model.answer: A compiler: it produces fast machine code and does not reveal the source code.

teach.heading: Check: interpreter
teach.note: Answer B. An interpreter translates and runs one line at a time, so it reaches an error in a later line only after running the earlier ones. A compiler (A, C) translates the whole program first. D mixes up an assembler and an interpreter.

check.q: Which translator would show output from the first lines of a program before it hits an error on line 40?
check.why: An interpreter translates and runs line by line, so earlier lines have already run. A compiler translates everything before running (A). An assembler translates assembly, not high-level code (C). Machine code is not a translator (D).

practice: State two advantages of high-level languages over low-level languages.
Explain one advantage of a compiler over an interpreter and one advantage of an interpreter over a compiler.
Name the translator for assembly language.
independent: Core: Complete a table comparing compiler and interpreter on how they translate, speed, error reporting and distribution.
Extend: A student is learning to program and testing small changes many times an hour. Choose a translator and justify.
Stretch: A washing machine controller has 2 KiB of memory. Discuss whether it should be programmed in a high-level or low-level language.
exit: What does an assembler translate?
Why is machine code described as processor-specific?
lessons.homework: Make a poster comparing high-level language, assembly and machine code with an example of each and a use for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a two-column sort of statements 'compiler' and 'interpreter'. Stretch: ask pupils to explain what a bytecode interpreter is.

lessons.unit: Unit 4.1: Networks: types, protocols and connections
lessons.title: Why network? LANs, WANs, the internet, IP addresses and routers
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a request from your device cross the world and come back in a fraction of a second?
objectives: Give reasons for connecting computers in networks (4.1.1)
Distinguish LAN and WAN (4.1.2)
Describe internet structure, including IP addressing and routers (4.1.3)
successCriteria: All: state two reasons for networking and distinguish a LAN from a WAN
Most: explain what an IP address is and what a router does
Some: describe how a packet travels across the internet and validate an IPv4 address
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: global connections and infrastructure
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the internet allows learning communities, like this online school, to meet across distance; with that comes responsibility for how we use it

keywords.def: two or more devices connected so that they can share data and resources
local area network: covers a small area and is owned by one organisation
wide area network: covers a large area, often using leased lines
a number that identifies a device on a network
a device that forwards packets between networks

starter: Bismillah. Name a piece of hardware that connects devices in a LAN.
How many values can 8 bits hold?
Name one device in your home that is connected to a network.

teach.heading: Why connect computers?
bullets: Share files, printers and an internet connection
Communicate by email, messaging and calls
Manage users, software and backups centrally
teach.note: Pupils usually say 'to go on the internet'; push them to name sharing resources, communication and central control. Link to the school: one printer for many pupils, one login on any computer. Give one drawback: if the network fails or is attacked, many users are affected.

left.title: LAN
points: Small area: a building or campus
Owned and managed by one organisation

right.title: WAN
points: Uses links leased from telecoms companies
The internet is the largest WAN

teach.heading: IP addresses
bullets: Every device on a network has an IP address
IPv4: four numbers from 0 to 255, such as 192.168.1.20
IPv6 has longer addresses so we do not run out
teach.note: Each IPv4 number is 8 bits, so 0 to 255, and four numbers give 32 bits. Link to 2.1: this is why 256 is invalid. IPv6 uses 128 bits and is written in hexadecimal. Run the validator: it checks four parts and that each is a number up to 255. A domain name is easier to remember; a system called DNS looks up the IP address for it.

teach.heading: Routers and the structure of the internet
bullets: The internet is a network of networks
Routers read the destination IP address
Each router passes the packet on towards its destination
teach.note: Draw a home network connected to an ISP, which connects to larger networks. A packet hops from router to router; no single router knows the whole route; each chooses the next hop. Packets in the same message may take different routes. Add that a home router also connects the LAN to the internet.
cycle: Device sends a packet with the destination IP address
Home router passes it to the ISP
Routers along the way choose the next hop
The last router delivers it to the destination network
The destination device receives and reassembles the packets

teach.heading: Worked example: explain a journey
teach.note: Model the language of the mark scheme: IP address, router, next hop, packets. Notice that the answer says what each does, not just names them. Ask pupils which step fails if the router is switched off at home (no link to the internet).

model.problem: Explain how a page request from a laptop in a school LAN reaches a web server abroad.
steps: The laptop puts the server's IP address on each packet as the destination
The packets go to the school router, which forwards them to the internet service provider
Each router on the way reads the destination IP address and passes the packet to the next router
The last router delivers it to the web server's network, and the server replies in the same way
model.answer: Packets are forwarded across several routers, using IP addresses, to the server and back.

teach.heading: Check: IP address
teach.note: Answer C. Each of the four numbers is 8 bits (0 to 255), so 300 is not valid. A is valid. B is valid. D has five parts. Pupils are asked to apply the 0 to 255 rule from binary.

check.q: Which of these is not a valid IPv4 address?
check.why: Each part must be between 0 and 255 (8 bits). 300 is too big. The other addresses all have four parts between 0 and 255.

practice: Give two reasons why a school connects its computers into a LAN.
State two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
Write the number of bits in an IPv4 address and explain why 256 cannot appear in one.
independent: Core: Draw a diagram of a home network connected to the internet, labelling the router, the ISP and a web server.
Extend: Use the validator code to say whether 192.168.1.0, 256.1.1.1 and 1.2.3.4.5 are valid IPv4 addresses and why.
Stretch: A packet from London to Cairo might travel through several routers by a different route each time. Explain two advantages of the internet working this way.
exit: What does a router do?
Write one valid and one invalid IPv4 address.
lessons.homework: Find your device's IP address (or use the pretend address 192.168.1.15) and write 100 words explaining what the number tells a network and what it does not tell.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a labelled map of the internet with arrows to follow and a word bank. Stretch: ask for a comparison of IPv4 and IPv6 with the number of addresses (2^32 and 2^128). The existing y11 lessons 5 and 6 introduce LAN, WAN and addresses; this lesson adds the reasons for networks and internet structure.

lessons.unit: Unit 4.1: Networks: types, protocols and connections
lessons.title: Wired and wireless connections: speed, range, latency and bandwidth
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a video call freeze in one room and run smoothly in another?
objectives: Explain how wired and wireless connections affect speed, range, latency and bandwidth (4.1.4)
Define bandwidth and latency and explain the difference
Recommend a connection type for a scenario
successCriteria: All: define bandwidth and latency
Most: compare wired and wireless connections on four factors
Some: justify the best connection for a scenario using the four factors and the number of users
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: waves, interference and signals in cables
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness (adl) in sharing a connection: one user's large download can slow others down

keywords.def: the maximum amount of data that can be sent each second
the delay between sending data and it arriving
the distance over which a connection works
signals from other sources that disrupt a transmission
a cable that carries data as pulses of light

starter: Bismillah. What does LAN stand for?
Give one benefit of Wi-Fi in a school.
Name one device that uses a cable to connect to a network.

teach.heading: Bandwidth and latency
bullets: Bandwidth: how much per second (bits/s)
Latency: how long a signal takes to arrive
A fast connection needs both high bandwidth and low latency
teach.note: Use the analogy of a road: bandwidth is the number of lanes, latency is the time for one car to get from A to B. Many pupils say 'speed' for both; insist they use the precise terms. Gaming and video calls are sensitive to latency; large downloads need bandwidth.

teach.heading: Wired and wireless
bullets: Wired: Ethernet cable or fibre
Wireless: Wi-Fi uses radio waves
Each affects speed, range, security and mobility
teach.note: Fibre uses pulses of light, so it has very high bandwidth and long range and is not affected by electrical interference. Copper Ethernet is cheaper, with a range limit of about 100 metres. Wi-Fi is convenient, but slower, shared and affected by walls, distance and other signals; its range and speed fall as you move away. Use the table for the comparison.

head: Factor
Copper cable (Ethernet)
Fibre optic
Wi-Fi
rows: Up to about 100 m per cable

teach.heading: Worked example: choose a connection
teach.note: Model by listing the needs first, then choosing. Show that both can be used in one network (wired for fixed devices, wireless for visitors). Note the common error of choosing wireless 'because it is faster': it is rarely faster than a good cable.

model.problem: A madrasah office has four fixed computers that stream live lessons, and visitors who use phones. Recommend connections.
steps: Fixed computers streaming live lessons need high bandwidth and low latency: use Ethernet cables
Cables are also more reliable and not shared with the air, so less interference
Visitors with phones need mobility: provide Wi-Fi
Keep the visitors' Wi-Fi separate so it does not slow the lessons
model.answer: Wired Ethernet for the four computers; Wi-Fi for visitors.

teach.heading: Check: latency
teach.note: Answer B. Latency is the delay. A is bandwidth. C describes range, D describes interference. Ask why a download can be fast but a video call still lags (high bandwidth, high latency).

check.q: A pupil's online game lags even though the connection is advertised as 100 Mbit/s. Which measure is most likely the problem?
check.why: Lag in a game is caused by delay, high latency. High bandwidth (A) and wired connections (D) do not cause lag; range (C) is a different measure.

practice: Define bandwidth and latency.
State two reasons why Wi-Fi may be slower than an Ethernet cable.
Explain why fibre optic cable is used for long-distance links.
independent: Core: Complete a table comparing wired and wireless connections on speed, range, latency and security.
Extend: A library has 30 tablets and 6 fixed PCs. Recommend a connection for each and justify.
Stretch: Ten people in one house start streaming video at the same time and each notices buffering. Explain what is happening in terms of bandwidth and how it could be improved.
exit: Give one situation where low latency matters more than high bandwidth.
State one advantage of wireless over wired.
lessons.homework: Test the connection in two different rooms (or use a speed test) and record download speed and latency. Explain the difference in 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a picture of the road analogy with labels. Stretch: ask for an evaluation of the drawbacks of each choice. The existing y11 lesson 5 mentions bandwidth and media; this lesson separates latency and compares connection types in detail.

lessons.unit: Unit 4.1: Networks: types, protocols and connections
lessons.title: Calculating transmission time, speed and file size
lessons.bigQuestion: How long will this download take, and can we send it in time?
objectives: Calculate transmission time, rate and file size from network speed in bits per second (4.1.5)
Convert between bytes and bits correctly
Use the three-way relationship to solve problems
successCriteria: All: calculate the time to send a file given its size in bits and the speed
Most: convert bytes to bits first and give the time
Some: rearrange the formula to find speed or file size and compare two connections
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: rates, units and standard form
lessons.smsc: Moral: careful, honest calculation: neither exaggerating nor underestimating what a system can do

keywords.def: the unit of network speed (bit/s); 1 Mbit/s is 1 000 000 bit/s
how long it takes to send data
the amount of data in a file
the speed of a connection

starter: Bismillah. How many bits are in 500 bytes?
State the formula: speed = distance / time. What is time in terms of distance and speed?

teach.heading: The relationship
bullets: time = file size / speed
speed = file size / time
file size = speed x time
teach.note: Draw the triangle: size on top, speed and time below. Units must match: file size in bits and speed in bits per second give time in seconds. In this course, network speeds are given in bits per second with the decimal prefixes of megabits (1 000 000) unless the question says otherwise; check what the paper states. File sizes are often given in bytes, so multiply by 8.

teach.heading: Calculating in Python
bullets: Convert the size to bits first
Divide by the speed in bit/s
Check the unit of the answer
teach.note: Run the code: 500 000 bytes is 4 000 000 bits; at 2 000 000 bit/s it takes 2 seconds. The second line finds file size: 20 Mbit/s for 30 seconds is 600 000 000 bits, which is 75 000 000 bytes. Python helps us check but the exam is on paper, so pupils need to be able to do it with a pencil.

code.text:
size_bytes = 500000
speed = 2000000
print(size_bytes * 8 / speed, "seconds")
print(20 * 1000000 * 30 / 8, "bytes")

teach.heading: Worked example: time and speed
teach.note: Model by writing the formula, then substituting with units. Show the conversion line explicitly. Ask pupils what happens to the time if the speed doubles (it halves). Warn about the trap of leaving the file in bytes.

model.problem: A 3 MB file (3 000 000 bytes) is sent over a 6 Mbit/s connection. How long does it take?
steps: Convert bytes to bits: 3 000 000 x 8 = 24 000 000 bits
Convert the speed: 6 Mbit/s = 6 000 000 bit/s
time = size / speed = 24 000 000 / 6 000 000
Check units: bits divided by bit/s gives seconds
model.answer: The transfer takes 4 seconds.

teach.heading: Check: finding speed
teach.note: Answer C. 40 Mbit is sent in 8 seconds: 40 / 8 = 5 Mbit/s. A divides the wrong way round. B multiplies, D forgets to convert from the size in megabits. Ask for the units of each wrong answer.

check.q: A file of 40 Mbit is sent in 8 seconds. What is the speed?
check.why: speed = size / time = 40 / 8 = 5 Mbit/s. 0.2 comes from dividing the wrong way (A); 320 from multiplying (B); 48 from adding (D).

practice: How many bits are in a file of 250 000 bytes?
A 12 000 000 bit file is downloaded at 3 000 000 bit/s. How long does it take?
A connection runs at 8 Mbit/s. How many bits can it send in 10 seconds, and how many bytes is that?
independent: Core: Calculate the time to send a 1 500 000 byte file at 4 Mbit/s.
Extend: A video is 90 000 000 bytes. Compare the download time at 12 Mbit/s with 60 Mbit/s and state the ratio.
Stretch: A school needs to send a 2.4 GB (2 400 000 000 bytes) backup overnight in no more than 4 hours. Calculate the minimum speed in Mbit/s.
exit: State the formula for transmission time.
Convert 6 MB (6 000 000 bytes) to bits.
lessons.homework: Time how long a real download takes, use its size and your answer to work out the speed in Mbit/s, and compare with a speed test.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a formula triangle and a conversion ladder, with the first step filled in. Stretch: ask for calculations with minutes and with mebibytes, noting the effect of the unit. Check the paper's own definition of M for network questions.

lessons.unit: Unit 4.1: Networks: types, protocols and connections
lessons.title: Protocols: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, TCP/IP, HTTP(S), FTP and email
lessons.bigQuestion: Who decides how two computers made by different companies talk to each other?
objectives: Describe the purpose of Ethernet, Wi-Fi, TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, POP3, SMTP and IMAP (4.1.6)
Explain why protocols are needed
Choose the correct protocol for a task
successCriteria: All: say what a protocol is and give three examples
Most: match each protocol to its purpose
Some: explain the difference between POP3 and IMAP and between HTTP and HTTPS for a scenario
lessons.crossCurricular: English: rules of conversation and register
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and trust: HTTPS protects people's information when sent

keywords.def: an agreed set of rules for communication between devices
HTTP with encryption
protocol for sending email
protocol that reads email on the server, keeping messages in sync across devices
protocol that downloads email to one device

starter: Bismillah. What is a packet?
What does a router use to decide where to send a packet?
Name one use of encryption.

teach.heading: Why protocols?
bullets: Devices from different makers must understand each other
Rules say the format, order and checks
Each protocol has a job
teach.note: Use the analogy of language: without a shared language, the message cannot be understood. The existing y11 lesson 6 lists the common protocols; today we assign each a precise job. Introduce the first group: Ethernet and Wi-Fi manage how devices in a LAN transmit data; TCP/IP manages the delivery across networks.

head: Protocol
Purpose
rows: Splits data into packets, addresses them and delivers them reliably
As HTTP but encrypted, so others cannot read it

teach.heading: Files and email
bullets: FTP: transfers files between computers
SMTP: sends email to the mail server and between servers
POP3 and IMAP: receive email
teach.note: POP3 downloads messages to one device, usually removing them from the server; IMAP leaves them on the server so every device shows the same mailbox. For a phone and a laptop, IMAP is the better choice. SMTP is only for sending. A common error: using POP3 to send mail.

teach.heading: Worked example: which protocol?
teach.note: Model: identify the job in the scenario, then name the protocol and give the reason. The same scenario can use several protocols together: HTTPS for the page, TCP/IP for delivery. Keep the answer short and exact.

model.problem: Name the protocol used for each task: (a) sending a report to a teacher's email server; (b) viewing a bank's website securely; (c) reading the same inbox on a phone and a laptop; (d) uploading a 200 MB video to a web server.
steps: (a) Sending email: SMTP
(b) Secure web page: HTTPS, because the data is encrypted
(c) Same inbox on two devices: IMAP, which keeps messages on the server
(d) Transferring a file: FTP
model.answer: (a) SMTP, (b) HTTPS, (c) IMAP, (d) FTP.

teach.heading: Misconception: HTTPS makes a site safe
bullets: HTTPS encrypts the data in transit
It does not prove the site is honest
Check the address and be careful
teach.note: A criminal can also use HTTPS on a fake site. The padlock tells you the connection is encrypted, not that the owner is trustworthy. Link to phishing in unit 5.3.

misconception.wrong: A website that uses HTTPS is always safe to give my details to.
misconception.right: HTTPS only means the data is encrypted between you and the site. A fraudulent site can also use HTTPS, so you still check who runs it.

teach.heading: Check: protocol selection
teach.note: Answer D. SMTP is used to send email. A is for receiving, B for web pages and C for files. Another way: ask 'which protocols receive' to build the full list.

check.q: Which protocol is used to send an email from your device to the mail server?
check.why: SMTP sends email. IMAP receives it and keeps it on the server (A). HTTP is for web pages (B) and FTP transfers files (C).

practice: State why protocols are needed.
Give one difference between HTTP and HTTPS.
A pupil reads email on a phone, a laptop and a tablet. Recommend POP3 or IMAP and explain.
independent: Core: Match nine protocols to their purposes in a table.
Extend: Describe, using at least three protocols, what happens when you send a photo by email and then view it on the web.
Stretch: Explain why a bank must use HTTPS, and why HTTPS alone is not enough to protect its customers.
exit: Which protocol sends email?
Which protocol is used to transfer a file to a server?
lessons.homework: Make a quick-reference card for all nine protocols with a one-line purpose and an everyday example for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a matching task with protocol cards and picture cards. Stretch: ask for a protocol choice for five new scenarios with reasons.

lessons.unit: Unit 4.1: Networks: types, protocols and connections
lessons.title: The four-layer TCP/IP model and packet switching
lessons.bigQuestion: How is a message wrapped, sent in pieces and put back together?
objectives: Describe the four-layer TCP/IP model (4.1.7)
Describe what each layer does and which protocols belong to it
Explain how data is split into packets, sent and reassembled
successCriteria: All: name the four layers in order
Most: state the job of each layer and give a protocol for each
Some: trace a message through the layers on sending and receiving
lessons.crossCurricular: English: structure and layers of communication
lessons.smsc: Moral: order and care in communicating (the message arrives complete)

keywords.def: one level of the network model with its own job
a small chunk of data with a header holding addresses and a sequence number
extra data at the front of a packet, such as addresses
splitting data into packets that may take different routes

starter: Bismillah. Name two protocols and what they do.
What does a router read on a packet?
State why a long message is divided into smaller parts.

teach.heading: Four layers
bullets: Application: the program's protocol (HTTP, SMTP, FTP)
Transport: splits data and checks delivery (TCP)
Internet: addresses and routes (IP)
Link: sends on the local network (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
teach.note: Say the layers top to bottom: application, transport, internet, link. Naming varies between textbooks (link is sometimes called network access): check the board's wording. Each layer only talks to the layer above and below, so a layer can be changed without changing the rest. Use a postal analogy: letter, envelope, sorting office, delivery van.

head: Layer
Job
Examples
rows: Provides the service the user wants
Splits data into numbered packets; checks and resends
Adds source and destination IP addresses; routes packets
Sends the bits over the local connection

teach.heading: Packets in code
bullets: Split the message into numbered packets
Packets can arrive in any order
The receiver sorts by number and rebuilds
teach.note: Run the simulation: four packets with sequence numbers. In real networks the sort step is done by the transport layer. Ask what happens if packet 2 never arrives (TCP asks for it to be sent again).

code.text:
message = "ASSALAMU ALAYKUM"
size = 4
packets = []
for i in range(0, len(message), size):
    packets.append((i // size, message[i:i + size]))
print(packets)
packets.reverse()
packets.sort()
result = ""
for number, text in packets:
    result = result + text
print(result)

teach.heading: Worked example: layers in action
teach.note: Model going down the layers on the sender's side and up on the receiver's side. Pupils should use the layer names and the verbs: splits, addresses, sends. The packet gains a header at each layer on the way down and loses it on the way up.

model.problem: Describe what happens at each layer when a laptop requests a web page using HTTPS.
steps: Application: the browser makes the request using HTTPS
Transport: TCP splits the data into numbered packets
Internet: IP adds the source and destination IP addresses
Link: Ethernet or Wi-Fi sends the packets across the local network, then the server reverses the steps
model.answer: Application, then transport, internet and link on the way out; the server reassembles on the way back up.

teach.heading: Check: which layer?
teach.note: Answer B. IP addressing belongs to the internet layer. A (application) provides services, C (transport) splits and numbers packets, D (link) sends over the physical connection.

check.q: At which TCP/IP layer are the source and destination IP addresses added to each packet?
check.why: The internet layer (IP) adds addresses and routes packets. The application layer provides the service (A), the transport layer numbers and checks packets (C), and the link layer sends them over the local connection (D).

practice: List the four layers of the TCP/IP model from top to bottom.
State two things TCP does when sending a large file.
Explain why packets might arrive out of order and how the receiver fixes this.
independent: Core: Draw a four-layer diagram and add a protocol and a job to each layer.
Extend: Write about 80 words describing the journey of an email, naming the layer at each stage.
Stretch: Explain two advantages of a layered model, for example when Wi-Fi is replaced with Ethernet.
exit: Which layer is TCP in?
Why are packets numbered?
lessons.homework: Create an analogy (not the postal one) for the four layers and explain each part.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a four-layer template with pictures and a word bank. Stretch: ask for the effect on the model if a new protocol replaces Wi-Fi.

lessons.unit: Unit 4.1: Networks: types, protocols and connections
lessons.title: Network topologies: bus, star and mesh
lessons.bigQuestion: How should we arrange the cables so the network keeps working when something fails?
objectives: Compare bus, star and mesh topologies (4.1.8)
Draw each topology and describe how data flows
Recommend a topology for a given situation, with reasons
successCriteria: All: draw and name the three topologies
Most: state one advantage and one disadvantage of each
Some: recommend and justify a topology for a scenario, including cost and reliability
