lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: planning layout and infrastructure
lessons.smsc: Moral: resilience: preparing so that the whole community is not harmed by one failure

keywords.def: the layout of devices and connections in a network
all devices connected to one shared main cable
every device connected to a central switch
devices connected to many other devices, giving multiple routes
a device that sends data only to the device it is intended for

starter: Bismillah. What device connects devices in a LAN?
Give one disadvantage of relying on a single cable.
Name the layer where Ethernet works.

teach.heading: Three layouts
bullets: Bus: one shared backbone cable
Star: all devices to a central switch
Mesh: many links between devices
teach.note: Draw all three on the board. In a bus, all data travels on one cable and every device sees it; collisions rise as more devices join. A star is the standard LAN design today because failures only affect one device. A mesh gives alternative routes; full mesh has a link between every pair of devices, so the number of links rises rapidly.

right.title: Star
points: One cable fault affects one device

teach.heading: Mesh and the comparison
bullets: Mesh: data can take alternative routes
Very reliable, but costly and complex
Wireless mesh is used for internet backbones and some homes
teach.note: A full mesh of n devices needs n(n-1)/2 links: 10 devices need 45 links. This is the reason for the cost. The table summarises. Ask which topology a school should choose for a computer room, then check against the table.

teach.heading: Worked example: recommend a topology
teach.note: Model by listing requirements then comparing. Show that the answer links features to the scenario. Add that a star with a switch also isolates traffic, which helps performance.

model.problem: A madrasah is setting up a computer room with 20 computers. It needs the network to keep working if one cable is damaged, and it has a modest budget. Recommend a topology.
steps: Requirement 1: a damaged cable must not stop everyone
Bus: a break in the backbone could stop all 20 computers
Mesh: very reliable but needs many links, so too costly
Star: a cable fault affects only one computer, and cabling cost is moderate
model.answer: A star topology, because it limits the effect of a cable fault at a reasonable cost.

teach.heading: Check: failure
teach.note: Answer C. In a bus, the one shared backbone is a single point of failure for the whole network. A and B describe mesh and star behaviour. D is a common mix-up between star and bus.

check.q: What happens if the main backbone cable of a bus network is cut?
options: Only one computer loses its connection
The network is split and may stop working
Nothing happens because there is a switch
check.why: All devices share the backbone, so a break can disconnect the network. Rerouting (A) is a feature of a mesh. Only one computer being affected (B) describes a star.

practice: Draw a star topology with six computers.
State one advantage and one disadvantage of a bus topology.
How many links does a full mesh of 6 devices have? (use n(n-1)/2)
independent: Core: Complete a table with advantages and disadvantages for bus, star and mesh.
Extend: A hospital needs a network that never goes down. Recommend a topology and justify, mentioning cost.
Stretch: A company with five offices connects each office to every other. Calculate the number of links, then compare with a star layout and discuss which to use.
exit: Name the central device in a star network.
Why is a mesh network more reliable?
lessons.homework: Draw the network in your home or school as a topology diagram and say which topology it is closest to and why.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give outline diagrams to label and a table to complete with key words. Stretch: ask for a calculation of the links for 12 devices. Existing y11 lesson 5 covers star and mesh; this lesson adds bus and a full three-way comparison.

lessons.title: Network security: penetration testing, access control, physical security and firewalls
lessons.bigQuestion: How do organisations test and defend their networks without breaking the law?
objectives: Identify network vulnerabilities through penetration testing and ethical hacking (4.2.1)
Explain access control and physical security (4.2.1)
Explain how a firewall protects a network (4.2.1)
successCriteria: All: define penetration testing and give two network protections
Most: explain how each protection works and what it prevents
Some: recommend a combination of protections for a scenario and explain how they work together
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: law and responsibility online
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah and permission: testing a system is lawful and ethical only with the owner's agreement; entering one without it is a crime and a breach of trust

keywords.def: authorised, simulated attacks on a system to find weaknesses
hacking with the owner's permission, to improve security
limiting who can reach data and what they can do
filters traffic in and out of a network using rules
locks, guards and other measures that protect hardware

starter: Bismillah. Name two types of malware.
State the purpose of a password.
What is the Computer Misuse Act 1990 about?

teach.heading: Finding weaknesses
bullets: Penetration testing: authorised, simulated attack
Ethical hacker has written permission from the owner
A report lists weaknesses to fix, then tests again
teach.note: An ethical hacker's actions are legal because the owner has agreed to a defined scope; unauthorised access breaks the Computer Misuse Act 1990. Contrast with a malicious hacker. The test finds weak passwords, unpatched software and badly configured devices. Ask: why test a system that seems fine? (You find the problem before a criminal does.)
cycle: Agree scope and permission in writing
Fix the faults and test again

teach.heading: Access control and physical security
bullets: Access control: accounts, passwords, access levels, biometrics
Physical security: locks, ID cards, CCTV, secure server room
Both protect data: one online, one in the building
teach.note: Access levels follow the principle of least privilege: each user gets only the rights needed for their job (pupils cannot open staff records). Strong password plus a second factor is stronger than a password alone. Physical measures matter because stolen hardware can leak data directly. Pupils often forget physical security in network answers.

teach.heading: Firewalls
bullets: Sit between a network and the internet
Check each packet against rules
Block unauthorised traffic; allow permitted traffic
teach.note: Run the program: it is a simplified firewall with a block list of source addresses (the addresses are in a range reserved for examples). Real firewalls use many kinds of rule and can also watch traffic leaving the network. A firewall does not stop a user opening a malicious attachment, so it is one layer of defence.

teach.heading: Worked example: a layered plan
teach.note: Model the idea of defence in depth: no single measure is enough. Pupils should name the measure, say how it works and what it prevents. Add a short evaluation at the end to earn the highest marks.

model.problem: A madrasah stores pupils' records on a server connected to the internet. Recommend four protections and explain each.
steps: Firewall: filters traffic and blocks unauthorised connections from the internet
Access control: staff have accounts with passwords and access levels, so only authorised staff open records
Physical security: the server is in a locked room with door entry, so no one can steal or tamper with it
Penetration testing: an ethical hacker, with permission, finds weaknesses to fix before criminals do
model.answer: A firewall, access control, physical security and penetration testing, working together as layers.

teach.heading: Check: ethical hacking
teach.note: Answer B. The key difference is permission. A is false, because the methods may be the same. C is not true, and D is a description of a malicious attacker. Stress the word authorised.

check.q: What makes the work of an ethical hacker different from that of a criminal hacker?
options: They have the owner's permission and report problems
They always keep the information they find
check.why: An ethical hacker works with the owner's permission, within an agreed scope, and reports weaknesses so that they can be fixed. The techniques may be the same (A).

practice: Define penetration testing.
Give two examples of physical security measures for a server room.
Explain what a firewall does.
independent: Core: Complete a table: protection, how it works, one threat it reduces, for four protections.
Extend: Explain why a firewall alone does not protect a network, using two examples of threats it does not stop.
Stretch: Evaluate (6 marks) the statement 'A small school does not need to pay for penetration testing.' Give arguments for both sides and reach a conclusion.
exit: What does an ethical hacker need before starting a test?
State one access control method.
lessons.homework: Write a security checklist for a mosque office computer containing donor records, using at least four measures from this lesson.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a matching task (measure, how it works, threat) and the cycle as a picture. Stretch: ask for a discussion of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and ethical hacking permission.

lessons.unit: Unit 5.1: Issues and impact: environmental effects
lessons.title: The environmental impact of computing
lessons.bigQuestion: Do the benefits of our devices outweigh their cost to the planet?
objectives: Discuss environmental impacts of computing: energy use, manufacture, replacement cycles and disposal (5.1.1)
Weigh the costs of devices against their benefits to give a reasoned view (5.1.1)
Structure a six-mark discussion answer
successCriteria: All: give impacts at manufacture, use and disposal
Most: explain how the impacts could be reduced
Some: write a balanced discussion with a justified conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: resource use, pollution and sustainability
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and moral: stewardship of the earth (khalifah); the Qur'an (7:31) warns against wastefulness

keywords.def: discarded electrical and electronic equipment
the amount of electricity used, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh)
meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
how often devices are replaced, often every few years

starter: Bismillah. Name one resource used to make a smartphone.
State what a data centre is.
Give one way a computer saves paper.

teach.heading: The life of a device
bullets: Manufacture: mining, materials, energy, water
Use: electricity for devices, networks and data centres
Disposal: e-waste, toxic materials, landfill, recycling
teach.note: Walk through the life cycle: this structure makes a good frame for a discussion answer. Manufacture uses metals such as copper and rare earths, and a lot of energy before the device is even switched on. Data centres use electricity for servers and for cooling. Old devices contain materials that can leak into soil and water if not disposed of properly, and valuable materials that can be recovered through recycling.

head: Stage
Environmental impact
Reduction
rows: Energy-efficient devices, renewable power, sleep modes

teach.heading: Calculating energy use
bullets: Energy (kWh) = power (kW) x hours
Power in watts divided by 1000 gives kW
Multiply by days to find yearly use
teach.note: Run the code: a 150 W desktop used 8 hours a day for 365 days. A laptop of 50 W would use a third as much. Ask pupils how switching off at night and using a more efficient device change the total. Note that most of the cost to the planet may be in manufacture rather than use for devices replaced often.

code.text:
watts = 150
hours_per_day = 8
days = 365
kwh = watts * hours_per_day * days / 1000
print(kwh, "kWh per year")
print(50 * hours_per_day * days / 1000, "kWh for a 50 W laptop")
code.output:
438.0 kWh per year
146.0 kWh for a 50 W laptop

teach.heading: Benefits as well as costs
bullets: Video calls and remote work cut travel
Smart meters and sensors reduce energy waste
Online learning and digital documents save paper and journeys
teach.note: A discussion needs both sides. For example, an online school such as TGA reduces journeys, but its pupils use devices and servers. Encourage pupils to weigh up: how big is each effect, and who decides? A strong answer reaches a conclusion that depends on how the technology is used.

left.title: Harm
points: Energy for data centres and devices

teach.heading: Worked example: plan a discussion answer
teach.note: Model the plan on the board before writing: claim, point, evidence, link to the question, then a conclusion with a judgement. The best answers give two sides and a reasoned view. In the exam this is worth six marks, so aim for three developed points.

model.problem: Discuss the environmental impact of schools replacing all laptops every two years. (Plan, 6 marks)
steps: Point 1 (harm): manufacture of 1000 laptops uses minerals and energy and creates waste
Point 2 (harm): old laptops become e-waste; toxic substances if not recycled
Point 3 (benefit): newer laptops are often more energy efficient and may suit new software
Counter: repair or upgrade, or a longer cycle, keeps the benefits with less harm
Conclusion: replacing every two years is hard to justify; four years with upgrades is better
model.answer: A balanced answer with developed points on both sides and a justified conclusion.

teach.heading: Check: reducing impact
teach.note: Answer C. Repairing and reusing a device reduces both manufacture and waste. A increases manufacture, B increases electricity, and D increases waste. Link to the idea of the replacement cycle.

check.q: Which action would most reduce the environmental impact of a school's computers?
options: Repairing and upgrading computers so they last longer
Throwing old computers into general waste
check.why: Keeping devices longer reduces manufacture and e-waste. Replacing every year (A), leaving machines on (B) and general-waste disposal (D) all increase the harm.

practice: State two environmental harms caused by the manufacture of devices.
A projector uses 300 W for 5 hours a day for 200 school days. Calculate the energy used in kWh.
Give one way a data centre could reduce its environmental impact.
independent: Core: Complete a table of impacts and reductions for manufacture, use and disposal.
Extend: Calculate the yearly energy use of 30 computers at 120 W for 6 hours a day for 190 days.
Stretch: Write a six-mark discussion: 'Online lessons are better for the environment than travelling to a school.'
exit: Define e-waste.
Give one environmental benefit of computers and one harm.
lessons.homework: Interview family members about what they do with old phones or computers. Write 150 words on what happens to them and how it could be improved.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a life-cycle diagram to label and sentence starters ('This harms the environment because...'). Stretch: ask for a conclusion that weighs the scale of each impact.

lessons.unit: Unit 5.2: Issues and impact: ethical, legal and ownership issues
lessons.title: Personal data: privacy, consent, ownership and data protection
lessons.bigQuestion: Who owns information about you, and what must organisations do to protect it?
objectives: Discuss privacy, consent, ownership and misuse of personal data (5.2.1)
Describe the main principles and rights in UK data protection law (5.2.1)
Apply the principles to a scenario and reach a reasoned view
successCriteria: All: define personal data and state two principles of data protection
Most: explain consent and give examples of misuse
Some: evaluate a scenario against the principles and recommend changes
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE and Citizenship: rights, privacy and online safety
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah: the Qur'an (4:58) tells believers to return trusts to those they are due; personal data is a trust

keywords.def: information that identifies a living person
a person's free, informed agreement to something
laws and practices that keep personal data safe and fairly used
the right to keep personal information to yourself
the person the data is about

starter: Bismillah. Give three examples of personal data.
State what is meant by encryption.
Why might a company want data about its customers?

teach.heading: Privacy, consent, ownership, misuse
bullets: Privacy: keeping personal information to yourself
Consent: free, informed agreement to data use
Misuse: selling, sharing or using it without permission
teach.note: Start with a concrete case: a free app collecting your location. Ask who owns the data, you or the company? Under data protection law you keep rights over data about you. Consent must be clear, not hidden in long terms. Misuse includes identity theft, discrimination and unwanted advertising.

head: Idea
Meaning
Example of a breach
rows: A child's photo published without permission
Pre-ticked boxes that join a mailing list
A company sells your details and refuses to delete them
Using data for harm or unfair purposes

teach.heading: UK data protection principles
bullets: Fair, lawful, transparent use
Collect only what is needed, for a stated purpose
Keep it accurate, secure and no longer than necessary
teach.note: Name the law: the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR. Pupils do not need section numbers but should know the principles. Rights include to see data held about you, to have errors corrected and, in some cases, erased. Organisations that break the law can be fined by the Information Commissioner's Office. Run the code to show data minimisation.

teach.heading: Worked example: evaluate a scenario
teach.note: Model by listing the principles and checking each against the scenario. The conclusion should recommend specific changes. Contrast what is lawful with what is ethical: even if the terms say yes, an unfair or hidden use may not be ethical.

model.problem: A fitness app collects users' heart rate, location and age, and sells the data to an advertising company without telling users clearly. Identify the problems and recommend changes.
steps: Consent: users were not clearly told, so their agreement is not informed
Purpose: the data was collected for fitness but used for advertising
Minimisation: location may not be needed for the service
Recommend: clear opt-in consent, collect only necessary data, never sell without permission, let users delete their data

Explain how algorithmic bias arises from data
Discuss accountability, safety and liability for automated decisions

Some: evaluate who is accountable in a scenario and reach a justified conclusion

keywords.def: a system that learns patterns from data instead of following only fixed rules
systematically unfair results because of biased data or design
being answerable for what a system does
legal responsibility for harm
a machine that can carry out tasks automatically

starter: Bismillah. What is an algorithm?
Give one example of a decision a computer makes for you.
State one advantage of automation.

teach.heading: How machine learning works
bullets: Learns patterns from lots of example data
Uses those patterns to predict on new cases
The quality of the data decides the quality of the result
teach.note: Give examples: spam filters, medical image analysis, recommendations. The system is only as good as its training data. Explain that the programmer does not write rules for each case; the system adjusts itself based on examples. This is why unexpected results can occur and why explanations are hard.

head: Use
Benefit
Risk

teach.heading: Where bias comes from
bullets: Learning from past decisions copies their unfairness
Missing groups in the data lead to poor results for them
Programmers' assumptions can be built in
teach.note: Run the code: in the past data, group A was approved 90 percent of the time and group B 10 percent. A model trained on this would learn to favour group A even if the groups are equally able. Emphasise that the computer is not 'neutral' just because it is a computer. Bias can be reduced by checking results for different groups and by using more balanced data.

teach.heading: Accountability, safety and liability
bullets: Accountability: who is answerable for the decision?
Safety: robots and AI must be tested and controlled
Liability: who pays if harm is caused?
teach.note: There may be several parties: the programmer, the company, the owner and the user. The law is still developing in some areas, so pupils should discuss options rather than state one answer. Safety includes keeping a human able to override, testing in realistic conditions and reporting failures.

left.title: Arguments for automation
points: Can be safer in dangerous jobs

right.title: Concerns
points: Hard to say who is responsible

teach.heading: Worked example: who is responsible?
teach.note: Model considering each party and the evidence, then reaching a view while accepting that it may depend on the facts. Mention that a human should be able to check important decisions. Encourage pupils to use phrases such as 'it depends on whether...'.

model.problem: A self-driving taxi hits a pedestrian because its software misread a road sign. Discuss who should be held accountable.
steps: The company that designed and sold the software: it was responsible for testing and safety
The programmers: they could have written and tested the code more carefully
The owner or passenger: only if they misused the vehicle
Overall: the company should usually be liable because it controls the design and profits from it
model.answer: The manufacturer is most likely to be accountable, though responsibility may be shared depending on the facts.

teach.heading: Check: bias
teach.note: Answer B. Learning from biased past data copies that bias. A, C and D describe things that are not causes of bias. Ask: what would you do to reduce bias? (Balanced data, testing for different groups, human review.)

check.q: A loan system trained on past decisions rejects most applicants from one area. What is the most likely cause?
options: The training data contained biased past decisions
check.why: A system that learns from past decisions will copy any unfairness in them. Computers have no feelings (A), and speed (C) or device age (D) are irrelevant.

lessons.bigQuestion: Who owns an idea, a photo or a program, and what are you allowed to do with it?

automatic legal protection for original creative work
protection for an invention, which must be applied for
protection for a name, logo or sign that identifies a brand
permission to use something under stated terms

Give one example of a program that is free to use.
State why it is wrong to copy someone else's homework.

teach.heading: Four protections
bullets: Copyright: written work, images, recordings, code
Patent: a new invention or process
Trademark: names, logos, slogans
teach.note: Pupils confuse these. Ask which would protect a poem (copyright), a new design of battery (patent) and a shop's logo (trademark). Copyright is automatic when the work is created; patents and registered trademarks must be applied for. Copyright lasts a long time (generally the life of the author plus many years); a patent usually lasts up to twenty years.

Protects
How obtained
Example

Terms for use of the work

teach.heading: Licensing
bullets: Proprietary: you pay and may not copy or modify
Open source: source code available to use and change
Creative Commons: owner states how it may be reused
teach.note: Open source does not mean 'no rules': licences still say what you can do, for example you may need to share changes. Free to download does not mean free to copy and sell. A licence is the owner's permission, so using work without one is infringement. Pupils should know the consequences: fines, legal action and removal of content.

left.title: Proprietary licence
points: You buy a licence to use it

right.title: Open-source licence
points: Source code can be seen and changed

teach.heading: Worked example: using someone else's work
teach.note: Model the question as a decision: is it protected, whose is it, what is the licence, what must you do? The right action is to ask or choose a work you may use. Ask pupils why crediting is not the same as permission.

model.problem: A pupil downloads a photo from a website and uses it on the school's public website without asking. Explain the problem and what they should do.
steps: The photo is protected by copyright automatically; the photographer owns it
Using it publicly without permission or a licence infringes the copyright
Giving credit is not the same as permission
They should ask the owner, use a photo with a licence that allows it, or take their own
model.answer: This is copyright infringement; the pupil should get permission or use a licensed or original image.

teach.heading: Check: choosing protection
teach.note: Answer C. A brand logo is protected by trademark. A (copyright) would protect the artwork of the logo, but the identification of a brand is a trademark. B protects an invention and D is not a protection.

check.q: A new company wants to stop others using its name and logo to sell products. Which protection should it register?
check.why: Trademarks protect names and logos that identify a brand. A patent (B) protects an invention. Copyright (A) is automatic for creative work, and an open-source licence (D) would allow others to reuse.

Give one difference between a patent and a trademark.
Explain one risk of using software without a valid licence.

State one condition that an open-source licence might impose.

a weakness in a system that can be exploited

Trojan: disguised as useful software
Ransomware, spyware, keylogger

teach.heading: Technical vulnerabilities
bullets: Out-of-date software with known flaws
Weak or default passwords
Unvalidated input, such as SQL injection
teach.note: Unvalidated input is the one pupils find hardest, so show it in code. The program builds a database query from what the user typed. An attacker types text that changes the meaning of the query: the condition '1'='1' is always true. This is why input is validated and queries are built safely. Also mention unpatched systems and weak passwords.

bullets: Phishing: fake emails or texts
Pretending to be someone trusted (blagging)
Shouldering: watching someone type a password
teach.note: Show how a simple filter could spot urgency words. It is not reliable, but it makes the point: attackers use urgency and fear. In real life, check the sender address, do not click links, and contact the organisation using a number you already trust. Phishing is the most common cause of data breaches.

teach.heading: Worked example: spot the threat
teach.note: Model by underlining the clue words in the scenario and naming the threat for each. Pupils should say how each works and one thing the user could have done. Add that more than one threat can be involved in one attack.

model.problem: An office worker receives an email that appears to be from IT: 'Your account is suspended. Click here and enter your password now.' After they do, files on the network become locked and a payment is demanded. Identify the threats.
steps: The fake email using urgency to get a password is phishing, a social engineering attack
The attacker uses the stolen password to get in
Files locked with a payment demand is ransomware, a type of malware
Weakness exploited: a trusting user; a second factor and training could have helped
model.answer: Phishing (social engineering) followed by ransomware (malware).

teach.heading: Check: malware type
teach.note: Answer A. A worm copies itself across a network without needing the user to run it. B (virus) needs a host file. C (trojan) disguises itself. D (spyware) records activity. Ask which of the four needs the user to be tricked.

check.q: Malware spreads from computer to computer across a school network with no action from any user. What is it?
check.why: A worm copies itself across networks on its own. A virus needs a host file to be run (B), a trojan relies on the user installing it (C), and spyware gathers information (D).

lessons.title: Protecting systems: anti-malware, encryption, policies and backup
lessons.bigQuestion: If an attack succeeds, how do we limit the damage and recover?
objectives: Explain protection methods: anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery (5.3.2)
Describe how encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext
Design a backup and recovery plan
successCriteria: All: name four protection methods
Most: explain how each protects a system or data
Some: design a layered plan and justify each measure

lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah: keeping other people's data safe is a duty, and backup guards against losing what others rely on us for

keywords.def: scrambling data so that only someone with the key can read it
readable data before encryption
the scrambled data after encryption
rules about how a system may and may not be used
a copy of data stored separately so it can be recovered

starter: Bismillah. Name two types of malware.
What is the purpose of a utility such as a firewall?
Calculate (24 + 5) mod 26.

teach.heading: Encryption
bullets: Plaintext is scrambled into ciphertext with a key
Without the key the data is unreadable
Used for HTTPS, messages and stored files
teach.note: The simple Caesar cipher shifts each letter along the alphabet. It is easy to break and not used for real security, but it shows the ideas of plaintext, ciphertext and a key (here the shift of 3). Modern encryption uses far more complex mathematics. Encryption does not stop theft; it makes stolen data useless without the key.

code.output:
PHHW DW IDMU
MEET AT FAJR

teach.heading: Anti-malware and acceptable use
bullets: Anti-malware scans for and removes malicious software
Keep it and the system up to date
An acceptable use policy sets rules for users
teach.note: Anti-malware compares files with known patterns and watches behaviour; it only knows about threats it has seen, so updates are essential. An acceptable use policy tells users what they may do on the school or work network and the consequences of misuse; it protects both users and the organisation. Add other methods: updates, strong and unique passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls.

teach.heading: Backup and recovery
bullets: Copy data regularly to a separate place
Store a copy off-site or in the cloud
Test that the backup can be restored
teach.note: A backup only protects you if you can restore from it, so recovery needs to be tested. A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies only what has changed since the last backup, so is quicker. Keeping a copy away from the original protects against fire, theft and ransomware. Ask: why is a backup on the same computer not enough?

teach.heading: Worked example: a recovery plan
teach.note: Model by combining prevention, detection and recovery. Link each choice to a risk. A complete answer includes testing and security of the backup itself (encrypted, access controlled).

model.problem: A madrasah stores pupils' records on one office computer. Describe a plan to protect against ransomware and hardware failure.
steps: Prevent: anti-malware kept up to date, software updates, an acceptable use policy and phishing training for staff
Back up: a daily incremental and a weekly full backup
Store a copy off-site or in the cloud, with the backup encrypted so that it cannot be read if stolen
Test: restore a sample regularly to prove that recovery works
model.answer: Layered protection plus regular, tested, encrypted, off-site backups.

teach.heading: Check: why encrypt?
teach.note: Answer B. Encryption does not stop a thief taking the data but makes it unreadable without the key. A is wrong because encryption does not stop access. C is wrong as encrypted data is still copied; D describes a backup.

check.q: A laptop containing pupils' records is stolen. The data on it was encrypted. What is the main benefit?
options: The thief cannot take the laptop
The data is unreadable without the key
The records are automatically backed up
check.why: Encryption turns the data into ciphertext that cannot be read without the key. It does not prevent theft (A), create a backup (C) or trace the thief (D).
